Brentwood.metaDescription: Raccoons, squirrels, skunks and bats in Brentwood, NH — rural roads off Route 125 and the Exeter River. Same-day service from our local crew.
Brentwood.housing_era: A rural town of colonial and Cape-style farmhouses along older roads, post-war ranches, and newer subdivisions set back in the woods off Route 125 and Route 111A.
Brentwood.geographic_features: Exeter River (flows through town, raccoon and beaver corridor), Route 125 corridor (main north-south road), Rockingham Recreational Trail (wooded rail trail), Great Brook (small tributary stream)
neighborhoods: Town center (historic homes near Route 125 and South Road)

Prescott Road area (rural homes in heavy woods)

Brentwood.wildlife_intro:
Brentwood stays rural even as Rockingham County grows around it, and that mix of farm fields, deep woods and scattered subdivisions keeps wildlife close to houses. Raccoons work the Exeter River corridor and get into chimneys and barns, gray squirrels chew into soffits on wooded lots, and skunks and woodchucks dig under sheds, decks and barn foundations. Bats roost in older farmhouse attics and outbuildings through summer.

Long winters push mice and squirrels inside early, and fall is when our crew hears most about animals looking for winter shelter. Spring brings young raccoons in chimneys and woodchucks back under outbuildings. Most Brentwood jobs pair removal with sealing the entry and checking the barn or shed nearby, because on rural lots the next den site is usually only a few yards away.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Brentwood, NH?
faqs.a: Cost depends on the animal, how it got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the home needs, so our crew inspects first and explains the options before any work starts.  Simple single-entry squirrel jobs cost less than full attic exclusion or bat work, and we never quote a firm figure before seeing the structure.

faqs.q: Why do woodchucks keep digging under barns and sheds in Brentwood?
faqs.a: Open fields, stone walls and loose soil around outbuildings give woodchucks easy digging and good cover. Once one burrows under a slab or foundation, others may reuse the site. Our crew removes the animal, checks for connected burrows, and talks through backfilling and barrier options so the next woodchuck does not move straight back in.

Winter here is long, so fall exclusion matters — once snow covers the roof, entry points are harder to seal well. Spring means raccoon mothers in chimneys and squirrels raising litters in attics. Our crew handles a lot of Derry work in that fall window, sealing soffits and chimneys before animals settle in for the cold months.

Salem.wildlife_intro:
Salem's mix of dense subdivisions, busy retail and wooded pockets produces a wide call mix. Norway rats turn up around dumpsters and older commercial blocks on Route 28 and follow food into nearby homes, while raccoons and gray squirrels work attics across the subdivisions. Skunks and opossums live under decks in the southern tier here, and bats roost in older Capes and ranches. Canobie Lake homes add shoreline raccoons and mice in seasonal properties.

Fall shelter-seeking is Salem's busiest season, when rats, mice and squirrels all test foundation and roofline gaps before winter. Spring litters in attics follow close behind. Our crew spends much of its Salem time on exclusion — sealing the gap matters more than removing one animal, because in these dense neighborhoods another one is always nearby.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Salem, NH?
faqs.a: Cost depends on the animal, how it got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the home needs, so our crew inspects first and explains the options before any work starts. faqs.q: Are rats a real problem in Salem, or just around restaurants?
faqs.a: Both. Route 28 food and dumpster areas support rat populations, and rats travel — nearby homes with bird feeders, pet food or foundation gaps get visits too. Our crew looks at food sources and entry points together, because trapping alone rarely holds in a commercial-adjacent neighborhood.

Londonderry.wildlife_intro:
Londonderry's orchards, fields and big conserved woods keep wildlife woven through its subdivisions. Raccoons and gray squirrels are the everyday attic call, skunks dig under decks and sheds, and moles tear up the well-kept lawns this town is known for. Homes backing onto the Musquash Conservation Area see fishers on trail cameras and steady pressure from the woods, and bats roost in older farmhouses and newer attic spaces alike.

Spring opens with woodchucks under outbuildings and squirrels raising young in attics, while fall brings the shelter-seeking rush before the long winter. Summer is mole season on irrigated lawns. Our crew does a lot of Londonderry exclusion work on subdivision homes where the woods start at the back fence — sealing has to account for pressure that never really lets up.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Londonderry, NH?
faqs.a: Cost depends on the animal, how it got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the home needs, so our crew inspects first and explains the options before any work starts. faqs.q: Something screams in the woods behind our house at night. Should we worry?
faqs.a: That sound is often a fisher or a red fox, both common around the Musquash and other Londonderry woods. They rarely approach people, but they will take unsecured chickens or outdoor pet food. Keep food inside, secure coops well, and call us if an animal starts denning under a deck or shed.

Portsmouth.geographic_features: Piscataqua River (tidal river and working waterfront), Great Bay estuary (tidal waters to the west), South Mill Pond (pond by the South End), Sagamore Creek (tidal creek in the south)

Portsmouth.wildlife_intro:
Portsmouth's age is its wildlife story. Centuries-old homes in the South End have settled foundations, old chimney flashing and layered rooflines that give bats, raccoons and gray squirrels multiple ways in, and bat colonies in historic attics are a defining summer call here. Norway rats work the waterfront and restaurant blocks downtown, mice are constant in multifamily buildings, and raccoons travel the Sagamore Creek and river corridors into residential streets.

Because so many Portsmouth homes are historic, our crew plans bat work carefully around the state rule — exclusion from occupied structures is not done from May 15 to August 15, when young bats cannot fly. Fall is the big sealing season before winter, and spring inspections catch problems before maternity colonies return to the same attics.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Portsmouth, NH?
faqs.a: Cost depends on the animal, how it got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the home needs, so our crew inspects first and explains the options before any work starts. Historic homes often cost more to seal because of multiple old entry points, and we explain that plainly after inspecting. Simple single-entry squirrel jobs cost less than full attic exclusion or bat work, and we never quote a firm figure before seeing the structure.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Portsmouth historic home?
faqs.a: Bats are exclusion-only in New Hampshire, and state rule prohibits excluding them from occupied structures between May 15 and August 15, when flightless young would be trapped inside. Our crew can inspect during that window, identify entries, and schedule the one-way exclusion for late summer or fall, when it can be done safely and legally.

Hampton splits between a busy beach strip and quieter year-round streets, and wildlife uses both. Skunks and raccoons live well around beach cottages, dumpsters and under raised decks, squirrels and mice move into cottages that sit empty all winter, and bats roost in older beach houses and inland attics. The salt marsh keeps raccoons traveling widely at low tide, and inland neighborhoods see the standard squirrel, skunk and woodchuck mix.

Spring camp and cottage openings are Hampton's signature season — owners return to droppings, nests and chewed openings after months away, and our crew does heavy inspection and cleanup work then. Fall is the other pinch point, sealing seasonal and year-round homes before animals claim them for winter. Year-round homes get steady raccoon and squirrel calls in between.

Exeter.wildlife_intro:
Exeter's historic downtown and academy neighborhoods hold older homes where bats, raccoons and gray squirrels are regular attic tenants. Settled chimneys, old soffits and big shade trees make entry easy, and the Squamscott and Exeter river corridors move raccoons and skunks through town. Newer subdivisions in the woods see squirrels, mice and woodchucks, and opossums appear under decks in this southern part of the state.

Our crew plans Exeter bat work around the May 15 to August 15 exclusion restriction, inspecting in summer and excluding in late summer or fall. Winter drives mice and squirrels deep into older homes, and spring brings raccoon families in chimneys. Most jobs here combine removal with careful sealing that respects older construction rather than covering it over.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Exeter, NH?
faqs.a: Cost depends on the animal, how it got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the home needs, so our crew inspects first and explains the options before any work starts.  Simple single-entry squirrel jobs cost less than full attic exclusion or bat work, and we never quote a firm figure before seeing the structure.

faqs.q: Do older Exeter homes really get more bat problems?
faqs.a: Yes. Original chimneys, layered additions and aging soffits give little brown and big brown bats many small gaps to use, and a colony tends to return to the same attic each summer. A full exterior inspection finds the entries, and exclusion outside the protected May 15 to August 15 window ends the cycle without trapping bats inside.
